newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech minister sees no stopping NATO enlargement.
newsitem.headline: Czech minister sees no stopping NATO enlargement.

text.p: Czech Foreign Minister Josef Zieleniec said on Thursday he saw no turning back on NATO enlargement but warned Russia and the West against competing for influence in Central Europe.
Zieleniec, speaking as Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin prepared to meet in Helsinki, said the eastward expansion of NATO would go ahead despite Russian opposition.

"I am confident of that. There is no turning back actually and this will also be an important step as regards the stabilisation of the security situation in Europe," Zieleniec told Reuters in an interview.

Enlargement of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) is the key topic for the Helsinki summit. The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are the leading candidates to be invited to join after an alliance summit in Madrid in July.
Russia bitterly opposes the expansion of the former Soviet Union's old Cold War foe on to territory once under the sway of the Moscow-dominated Warsaw Pact.
Zieleniec said he hoped the summit would help build trust between Russia and the West but cautioned both sides against playing power games in post-Communist Central Europe.

"It is important to clearly state and to make it clear that the central European space is not a space in which Russia and the West should contest for power and influence. Such an idea is quite unacceptable for us," he said.
But he said that leaving Central Europe without a clearly defined security structure could cause problems.
"This situation would generate a certain tension, a feeling of nervousness between East and West and the sooner this situation is terminated the better," he said.

Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati, due to meet Zieleniec on Friday, expressed similar views on Wednesday, saying in London that it would be dangerous to leave Central Europe as a grey zone because Russia did not pose a threat now.
East Europeans, conscious of Moscow's concerns, have stressed the political rather than military aspects of NATO membership.
"This is not only a security question, especially in these days. We live in a quite secure part of Europe and in quite secure times," Zieleniec said.

"It is a broader question connected above all with a strong feeling of identification with the values that the alliance protects, with our way of life and with the history which we shared with countries which are part of NATO," he added.
However, some officials acknowledge that NATO expansion is also a chance to anchor a region under Soviet domination for half a century after World War Two firmly with the West.

Warsaw Pact forces intervened in former Czechoslovakia in 1968 to put down the brief "Prague Spring" liberalisation movement while in 1956, Soviet troops crushed against the Hungarian Stalinist government, killing several thousand.

"Having had the experience we have had, we do not intend to give up any part of our sovereignty to that process, to transform the process of enlargement into a dual key issue which the Russians would necessarily have to approve," another leading Czech politician said on condition of anonymity.
Czech officials this week condemned remarks by Moscow's ambassador to Prague, Nikolai Ryabov, that key bilateral agreements could be jeopardised if the Czechs joined NATO.
But Zieleniec said he did not believe ties with Moscow should be affected. "It is not in the interests of our country, it is not in the interests of Russia," he said.
"Nevertheless, the beginning may be rather complicated," he added, saying this would depend on the atmosphere in which enlargement took place.
